chunks.text: Decision-native (“System One”) models. System One models return a typed, normalised distribution over a candidate set supplied at run time instead of generated text [ 7 ] . Since September 2026 the idea has been benchmarked on general tasks [ 8 ] , formalised [ 12 ] , extended to bi-encoders and smaller multimodal models [ 13 , 9 ] and to visual choice tasks [ 14 , 15 ] , and approximated without training by reading the letter logits of instruction-tuned models [ 16 ] , which we use as a baseline. Visual Jev [ 15 ] reads answer probabilities from the language-model head of a vision–language model and reports no consistent accuracy advantage for a typed decision head on general vision benchmarks, a reminder that the effect of the head is hard to separate from that of training. OmniMed-Jev [ 10 ] adapted the recipe to medical imaging and reported calibration gains over a matched generative baseline; its histopathology coverage is limited to PathMNIST. Medical evaluations of System One models are otherwise text-only [ 17 , 18 ] or zero-shot on ultrasound [ 19 ] , and Wienholt et al. [20] read single-pass yes/no decision scores from MedGemma and Gemma-3 without training. Risk-controlled thresholds for such scores are studied in [ 21 ] . To our knowledge no decision-native model has been trained or evaluated for histopathology with contamination-aware test sets. Pathology vision–language models. Contrastive models such as PLIP [ 22 ] and CONCH [ 1 ] enable zero-shot classification, zero-shot segmentation maps [ 23 ] , text-based interpretable embeddings [ 24 ] and concept-based explanations of slide classifiers [ 25 ] ; general VLMs have also served as zero-annotation tissue segmenters [ 26 ] . Contrastive scores are similarities whose softmax temperature is arbitrary, and they offer no explicit “none of these” answer. Generative assistants such as PathChat [ 2 ] answer in free text; their confidence is a token probability, not a decision probability.

Calibration studies of medical VLMs report that miscalibration is particularly severe in pathology [ 3 , 4 ] , and that explicit abstention options help [ 27 ] . 3 Method In this section we describe PathJev. We first define the typed decisions it answers, then the model that turns an image and a run-time candidate set into a distribution over the candidates, and finally the training recipe; Figure 1 gives an overview. Figure 1: Overview of PathJev. (1) Expert labels of six training sets from three public collections are turned deterministically into typed decisions: a patch carries a Choice (one of K K candidates, including “none of these”), Noul (yes/no) and Score (ordered levels) question; the orange candidate is the label. (2) The image is encoded by MedSigLIP and enters the Gemma-3 decoder as tokens, followed by the question and all candidates, each closed by a marker token. One forward pass yields hidden states at the markers; a decision head shared by all questions sums a per-candidate score, a question–candidate interaction and a set-attention term, and a softmax returns the distribution. A generative read-out, as implemented here, needs one forward pass per candidate. Training: Stage A fits the head on the frozen 4-bit backbone; Stage B adds LoRA adapters. Whole-slide use is shown in Figure 3 . Patches: SICAPv2 (CC BY 4.0). Bar heights in (2) are illustrative. 3.1 Typed decisions over runtime candidate sets We use the decision interface of System One models [ 7 ] , in the medical form of Tang and Chen [10] . A state is an image (here a single histology patch) together with one or more decisions . A decision D = ( Q , T , C ) D=(Q,T,C) consists of a question Q Q , a type T T and a finite candidate set C = { c 1 , … , c K } C=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{K}\} that is part of the model input rather than the index set of a fixed classifier. Three types are used: Choice (one of K K mutually exclusive candidates, e.g.

the tissue class of a patch), Noul (a Bernoulli decision { no , yes } \{\text{no},\text{yes}\} , e.g. “is tumour present?”) and Score (an ordered grid of levels, e.g. a Gleason grade group or a neoplasia level). For every decision the model returns a normalised distribution over its candidate set; one forward pass answers all decisions attached to a state. 3.2 Model The backbone is MedGemma-1.5-4B [ 11 ] , loaded in 4-bit NF4 precision. Candidate texts are written into the prompt after the image, each candidate closed by a key marker token and each question by a query marker token. One forward pass yields the last hidden states; a single decision head f ϕ f_{\phi} , shared by all questions and decision types, reads the (layer-normalised) hidden state k j ​ k k_{jk} at each candidate marker and q j q_{j} at the question marker and returns one logit per candidate as the sum of three terms: a per-candidate linear score w ⊤ ​ k j ​ k w^{\top}k_{jk} , a question–candidate interaction ⟨ W q ​ q j , W k ​ k j ​ k ⟩ / d \langle W_{q}q_{j},W_{k}k_{jk}\rangle/\sqrt{d} , and a set-attention term through which the candidates of one question attend to each other (multi-head attention with d = 128 d=128 , conditioned on log ⁡ K \log K ), z j ​ k = f ϕ ​ ( q j , k j ​ 1 , … , k j ​ K ) k , p j ​ k = exp ⁡ z j ​ k ∑ l exp ⁡ z j ​ l , z_{jk}=f_{\phi}\!\left(q_{j},\,k_{j1},\dots,k_{jK}\right)_{k},\qquad p_{jk}=\frac{\exp z_{jk}}{\sum_{l}\exp z_{jl}}, (1) so that no projection onto the language-model vocabulary is needed. All decision types share one objective, the cross-entropy between the target distribution y j y_{j} induced by the annotation and the predicted p j p_{j} , averaged over the M M decisions in a batch: ℒ = − 1 M ∑ j ∑ k y j ​ k log p j ​ k \mathcal{L}=-\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{j}\sum_{k}y_{jk}\log p_{jk} . Choice and Noul targets are one-hot; Score targets are one-hot on the annotated level.

3.3 Training recipe The decision head, the objective and the two-stage schedule follow Tang and Chen [10] ; what is specific to PathJev-P is the data, described in Section 4 . Stage A trains the head alone for 200 optimiser steps with the backbone frozen. Stage B trains the head together with LoRA adapters (rank 16, α = 16 \alpha=16 , dropout 0.05, all linear layers of the vision encoder and of the language model). Images are resized to 896 × 896 896\times 896 pixels; Choice candidates are shuffled at every presentation so that the model cannot rely on position, while Score candidates keep their order, which encodes the level. The effective batch is 32 states (8 per device, 4 accumulation steps). The learning rate and number of epochs are selected on validation data (Section 5.1 ). We call the resulting patch-level model PathJev-P . Input construction. Every state of a source carries the same list of questions, in the same order and with the same candidate lists, whatever its class; the target is never part of the input, and the prompt header carries no dataset name. The text of a test prompt is therefore constant within a test set, and the model’s answer to the main question can differ between images only through the image. The question wording does name the organ (e.g. “this prostate tissue”), so the auxiliary organ question is answerable from the text; it is not an endpoint and is reported nowhere, but it enters the validation loss used for checkpoint selection. Selecting on the main Choice question alone would pick the same checkpoint in every run (12 runs) and the same configuration for both methods. 3.2 Model The backbone is MedGemma-1.5-4B [ 11 ] , loaded in 4-bit NF4 precision. Choice and Noul targets are one-hot; Score targets are one-hot on the annotated level. 5 Experiments In this section we first describe the compared methods, model selection and evaluation, then compare PathJev-P with the baselines, analyse its calibration, including how the comparison with the generative model depends on the way that model’s probabilities are read out, and finally illustrate its use on whole slides. 5.1 Setup Compared methods. All methods answer the same questions about the same images, with the same candidate sets and candidate texts. (a) OmniMed-Jev [ 10 ] , the released decision-native checkpoint, used zero-shot.

It tells us how far a general medical decision model already goes on histopathology; since it differs from PathJev-P in training data, training length, model selection and input pre-processing, the comparison is between two systems. (b) Generative SFT. The same backbone and LoRA configuration, fine-tuned on the same training states to generate the answer text, with every decision of a state turned into one training example that lists the candidates as options. Its probability for a candidate is the softmax, over the candidate set, of the summed log-probability of the candidate’s tokens given the image and the prompt, the read-out used by OmniMed-Jev; one forward pass is needed per candidate. Both trained methods search the same grid and use the same selection rule, but they differ in objective, in the number of supervised targets and in optimiser steps (Appendix D ), so the comparison is between two systems rather than an ablation of the decision head. (c) CONCH [ 1 ] , a contrastive pathology vision–language model, used zero-shot with an ensemble of five prompt templates per candidate. (d) Linear probe on H-optimus-0 features [ 38 ] , trained on the labels of the training sets. Where a test question has no training labels (HepatoBench, HiESD), the probe is fitted on part of the test set itself by nested, grouped cross-validation. It is therefore a supervised reference, not a competitor. (e) Inner-Jev read-out [ 16 ] : the base MedGemma-1.5-4B, zero-shot, with the candidates listed as lettered options and the distribution read from the next-token probabilities of the letters. Implementation details of every method are in Appendix D . Model selection.

For PathJev-P and the generative baseline we search learning rates { 1 , 2 } × 10 − 4 \{1,2\}\times 10^{-4} and 3 or 5 epochs with one seed, keep the checkpoint and configuration with the lowest validation negative log-likelihood (NLL) on the Choice questions, and train the selected configuration with two further seeds. Only the validation mix (2,100 states) is used; no test data enters any choice of checkpoint, configuration, prompt or candidate wording. Evaluation. We evaluate the main Choice question of each test set (tissue class, lesion subtype or Gleason pattern) with balanced accuracy and expected calibration error (ECE; 15 equal-width bins on the top-candidate confidence), averaged over the clean test sets and reported separately for the unseen organs and the in-domain sets. Negative log-likelihood, Brier score, macro-F1, adaptive ECE, the area under the risk–coverage curve and reliability diagrams [ 30 , 31 ] complement them. Confidence intervals are 95% intervals of a paired cluster bootstrap that resamples patients (slides or images where patients are not identified) within each test set, and the trained methods are compared seed by seed. The hypotheses, endpoints, test sets and tests were fixed in an analysis plan before any test-set evaluation; analyses added later are labelled post hoc. Appendix A gives the statistical procedure, the plan and its amendments. The paired difference is +0.049 [+0.038, +0.063] against the generative baseline and +0.196 [+0.161, +0.218] against CONCH, and it favours PathJev-P in each of the three seeds. Its probabilities are also better calibrated than those of the four comparators (a), (b), (c) and (e), with the read-outs fixed in the analysis plan: the ECE is 0.204 ± \pm 0.002 against 0.279 for the generative baseline (difference -0.075 [-0.088, -0.064]) and 0.403 for CONCH (-0.199 [-0.237, -0.158]). These were the two hypotheses of the plan. The accuracy result is robust; the calibration result against the generative baseline depends on how that model’s probabilities are read out (Section 5.3 ). The released OmniMed-Jev often answers “other”. Removing that candidate raises its balanced accuracy, but it stays far below PathJev-P (Table 2 ), and its weakness is not a matter of input size: with images pre-resized to 896 instead of 448 pixels it reaches 0.207.

On the two organs absent from training, PathJev-P reaches a balanced accuracy of 0.390, against 0.277 for the generative baseline and 0.328 for CONCH. On the in-domain sets the two trained methods are close (0.692 and 0.707), and on the seen-source SPIDER sets the generative baseline is slightly ahead (0.810 against 0.781). Set by set (Appendix C ), PathJev-P is more accurate than the generative baseline on both unseen organs, whereas its advantage over CONCH comes from HepatoBench; on HiESD, CONCH is slightly more accurate. The secondary metrics and the Noul and Score questions show the same pattern (Appendix F ). The comparisons keep their sign when HepatoBench, whose images cannot be grouped by slide, is removed: the difference in balanced accuracy against the generative baseline is then +0.033 [+0.018, +0.052] (Appendix E ). Even so, accuracy on new organs remains modest, and on HiESD, with ten gastric classes, it is low for every language-model-based method (Appendix C ). Two post-hoc checks (Appendix E ) support this comparison. The order in which the candidates are listed matters little for PathJev-P: over 10 random orders, its clean balanced accuracy stays between 0.542 and 0.549, although 7.3% of individual predictions change. The generative baseline behaves similarly, while OmniMed-Jev changes 18.9% of its predictions. Finally, with every image replaced by a uniform grey image, PathJev-P and the generative baseline give one prediction per test set and their balanced accuracy falls to chance, so the question text, which is the same for every image of a set, does not by itself separate the classes. The linear probe on H-optimus-0 features answers a different question: how well a classifier does when it is trained on labels of the task. On the in-domain sets, where it is trained on the same labels as PathJev-P, the two are comparable in balanced accuracy (0.677 for the probe) but the probe is better calibrated (ECE 0.074).

On the seen-source sets it is far ahead (0.905), and on the unseen organs, where it is fitted on labelled patches of the test domain itself, it reaches 0.772. Where labels for a fixed question exist, a probe remains the stronger tool. 5.3 Calibration The generative baseline’s probabilities are reconstructed from the log-likelihoods of the candidate texts, and the way this is done is a choice. In a post-hoc check (Appendix E ) we therefore repeated the comparison with two other read-outs. Dividing each candidate’s summed log-likelihood by its number of tokens leaves the generative baseline’s balanced accuracy almost unchanged (0.492 on the clean sets, 0.289 on the unseen organs) but changes its calibration substantially (Table 10 ). Its clean ECE becomes 0.201, similar to PathJev-P’s 0.204, with a lower NLL (1.508 against 1.586); on the unseen organs it becomes better calibrated than PathJev-P (ECE 0.110 against 0.301), and in domain worse (0.293 against 0.108). Adding the probability of the end-of-answer token changes nothing. The calibration advantage of PathJev-P over the generative model therefore holds for the read-out used by OmniMed-Jev and fixed in our plan, but not in general; its accuracy advantage holds for every read-out. A single temperature fitted on the validation mix lowers the clean-set ECE of every method (per set in Table 15 ; PathJev-P 0.204 → \to 0.154, generative baseline 0.279 → \to 0.211). For the zero-shot models the fitted temperatures are large and flatten their outputs, which lowers their ECE (CONCH 0.403 → \to 0.086) without making them more discriminative.

Measured by NLL, which rewards both, PathJev-P is the best language-model-based method on the clean sets after scaling (1.399 against 1.597 for CONCH and 1.795 for the generative baseline). On the unseen organs, however, scaled CONCH reaches a lower NLL (1.769 against 2.079): the reliability diagrams (Figure 2 ) show that every model is over-confident on these organs, and a temperature fitted on the training domains does not correct this for PathJev-P. In a post-hoc analysis we fitted the temperature on different data (Table 3 ). A temperature fitted on one unseen organ and applied to the other lowers PathJev-P’s NLL on the unseen organs from 2.079 to 1.781, close to the 1.713 of an oracle fitted on the evaluated set itself. With two organs this is an observation, not a transfer property, but it suggests that labelled data from one new organ can correct much of the over-confidence on another. What the comparison shows. Trained on the same states with the same backbone, PathJev-P is more accurate than a generative model that scores the candidate texts, and the gain lies on the organs absent from training. The two systems differ in more than the decision head (objective, number of supervised targets, optimiser steps), so the gain cannot be attributed to the head alone; one explanation, which we have not tested, is that the head is trained directly on distributions over candidate sets, whereas the generative distribution is only assembled at test time from text log-likelihoods. The calibration comparison is less clear-cut: PathJev-P is better calibrated than the generative model under the summed read-out used in previous work, but not under a length-normalised one. Calibration advantages of decision-native models over generative baselines should therefore be reported for more than one read-out. A practical difference remains in any case: PathJev-P answers in one forward pass, the generative read-out in one pass per candidate. When to use it.

On new organs PathJev-P is over-confident, and a temperature fitted on the training domains does not correct this; in our post-hoc analysis, labelled data from one new organ corrected most of it on the other, which suggests a cheap remedy that remains to be tested on more organs. Where labels for a fixed question exist, a linear probe on a pathology foundation model is the better tool: it is better calibrated in every setting and far more accurate with target-domain labels. The case for a decision-native model is the open-vocabulary, label-free setting, such as naming tissue clusters in whole slides, where our demonstration shows that cluster-level labelling with abstention is feasible for coarse questions; its accuracy on fine-grained classes of new organs (0.390 balanced accuracy) is not yet sufficient. Limitations. All states are single patches, and the whole-slide pipeline was not evaluated systematically against pathologists. “Clean” means no documented overlap with the backbone’s training data, which is partly undisclosed. Only two organs are unseen, HepatoBench images cannot be grouped by slide or patient, and SPIDER only by slide. We used one backbone in 4-bit precision, one wording per candidate and one prompt ensemble for the zero-shot models, and the generative baseline was scored only on the capped test sets. OmniMed-Jev is run with the 448-pixel pre-resize of its inference code (the processor then rescales to 896 pixels); because it often selects “other”, it is also reported with that candidate removed and with one fixed random permutation of the candidates. Generative SFT : every Choice, Noul and Score decision of a training state becomes one example, which gives 170,390 examples. The step budget is pinned to PathJev-P’s largest Stage B budget (the “5 epochs” of the grid count passes over states); the selected checkpoint has made 0.94 passes over its examples, i.e. it has seen each decision about once, whereas the selected PathJev-P checkpoint has seen every state, with all its decisions, twice, with fewer optimiser steps (Table 7 ). At test time a candidate c c with tokens t 1 . . t n t_{1}..t_{n} is scored by s c = ∑ i log ⁡ p ⁡ ( t i ∣ image , prompt , t < i ) s_{c}=\sum_{i}\log p(t_{i}\mid\text{image},\text{prompt},t_{<i}) , without an end-of-answer token and without length normalisation, and p ⁡ ( c ) = softmax c ​ ( s c ) p(c)=\mathrm{softmax}_{c}(s_{c}) ; no candidate text is a prefix of another in any test question. CONCH : the L2-normalised text embeddings of the five prompts are averaged, and probabilities are the softmax of the model’s learned logit scale times the cosine similarity with the projected image embedding. Linear probe : the feature scaler, regularisation strength and temperature are chosen by grouped cross-validation on the training data; on HepatoBench and HiESD they are fitted, in each of five grouped outer folds, by inner grouped cross-validation on the outer training part only, with HiESD folds grouped by patient.

HepatoBench images cannot be grouped by slide, so patches of one slide can fall on both sides of a fold there; regrouping in blocks of consecutive images changes the probe’s balanced accuracy only slightly (Appendix E ). Inner-Jev : probabilities are renormalised over the option letters; every letter is a single token, and the largest candidate set has 25 options.
